akustik.title: 🎶 The Acoustics Adventure 🥁
akustik.subtitle: Hello Tone Master! Set your ears to receive, we are diving into the invisible and loud world of sound!

sections.title: 1. Origin: Everything vibrates!

quizzes.question: How is a tone or a sound created in the first place?

answers.text: Through invisible magic in the air.

sections.content:
Whether you speak, clap your hands, or pluck a guitar – sounds are always created by only one thing: Movement! An object wobbles back and forth at lightning speed. Physicists call this vibration. When your vocal cords vibrate in your throat, your voice is created. Place your hand on your larynx while speaking – you can feel the jittering!

📖 The Smart Dictionary: The Sound Source
The thing that jitters and creates the sound is called the sound source. This can be the skin of a drum, the string of a violin, or the metal sheet of a tuning fork.

🪛 The Magic Tuning Fork

sections.title: 2. The Medium: The Silent Emptiness of Space

quizzes.question: Why can't you hear any external sounds in spacesuits in space?

answers.text: Because the helmets are too thick.
Because in the vacuum of space, there are no air particles to carry the sound.

sections.content:
Imagine you are standing on the moon and a huge meteorite crashes silently into the ground. Silently? Yes! For the sound from the tuning fork to reach your ear, it needs tiny "postmen". These are the air particles. The tuning fork pushes the air, the air particles push their neighbors, and so the sound wave travels to your ear.

📖 The Smart Dictionary: The Vacuum
Sound always needs a substance (a medium) to propagate. This can be air, but also water or even iron! Where there is absolutely nothing at all – like in space – it is called a vacuum. Without air particles, there is no one to carry the sound further. In space, no one can hear you scream!

🌌 The Vacuum Lab (The Bell Jar)

An alarm clock is ringing inside the bell jar. Pump the air out!

{{QUIZ_q2}}

sections.title: 3. The Oscilloscope: Pitch and Volume

quizzes.question: What do you have to do on the oscilloscope to make the sound really DEEP (like a bear growl)?

answers.text: Decrease the frequency (fewer and wider waves).

sections.content:
Scientists want to see sound waves! For this, they use a microphone computer called an oscilloscope. It paints the invisible sound waves as jagged lines (wave crests and wave troughs) on a screen.

📖 The Smart Dictionary: Frequency & Amplitude
- Frequency (Pitch): How often does the wave vibrate per second? If it vibrates very quickly (many narrow waves), the tone is high like the squeak of a mouse. If it vibrates slowly, the tone is deep like the growl of a bear. This is measured in Hertz (Hz).
- Amplitude (Volume): How strongly does the wave swing out? If the wave crests are huge and high, the tone is loud. If they are tiny and flat, the tone is quiet, like whispering.

📺 The Wave Lab

Control the mixing console and watch how the sound wave changes!





{{QUIZ_q3}}

sections.title: 4. Speed of Sound: The Great Race

quizzes.question: You see lightning and count exactly 6 seconds until it thunders. How far away is the storm?

sections.content:
Sound is fast, but light is the absolute lightning champion! Light races around the entire earth almost 8 times in one second. Sound only manages "only" 340 meters per second in air. That's why in a thunderstorm we always see the lightning first and only seconds later does the thunder crash in our ears!

📖 Calculating with the Thunder Trick:
Since sound takes about 3 seconds for 1 kilometer, you can calculate: Count the seconds between lightning and thunder. Divide the number by 3. The result is the distance of the storm in kilometers! (If you count 9 seconds: 9 ÷ 3 = 3 kilometers away).

⚡ The Thunderstorm Simulator

sections.title: 5. The Echo: Sound Bounces Back!

quizzes.question: How does a bat find its prey at night?

answers.text: It has huge eyes that glow in the dark like flashlights.
It emits ultrasound and listens for the echo that bounces off the insect.

sections.content:
Do you remember how light particles bounce off a mirror like rubber balls? Sound waves do that too! When you shout loudly in the mountains, the sound waves fly off, bounce against the hard rock wall, and come back to you. We call this an echo (reflection of sound).

📖 Animals with Superpowers: Sonar
Bats hunt in the dark. They call out very high (ultrasound, so high that we humans cannot hear it). The sound bounces off a tiny mosquito and throws back an echo. The bat's ear calculates in a flash: Aha, the echo is coming from the right and was there quickly – the mosquito is close! This is called echolocation (or sonar in submarines).

🦇 The Bat Hunt

Help the bat to locate the moth in the dark!

{{QUIZ_q5}}

sections.title: 6. Resonance: When Tones Destroy Things!

quizzes.question: Why is the thick wooden box on a guitar important?

answers.text: It only serves so that you can hold the guitar better.
It is a resonance body and amplifies the quiet tone of the strings.

sections.content:
Have you ever seen an opera singer make a glass shatter with only her voice? That's not a trick! Everything in the world has its own "favorite vibration" (natural frequency). If a tone hits exactly this frequency, the object suddenly starts to vibrate wildly along with it. This vibrating-along is called resonance.

📖 The Guitar Box (Resonance Body)
A guitar string alone sounds very quiet. But it is stretched over a large wooden box (the guitar). The string forces the wood and the air in the box to vibrate along in the same rhythm. This resonance body makes the tone loud and powerful!

🍷 The Singing Glass

Use the controller to find exactly the natural frequency of the glass (at 4.0). When it lights up green, you have resonance!

arbeit.title: 👷 The Physical Work Adventure 🏗️
arbeit.subtitle: Hello future physicists! Get ready, today we clarify what "work" really means in physics!

sections.title: 1. What is "Work"? No Homework!

quizzes.question: You push with all your might against a thick tree for 10 minutes, but it doesn't move a millimeter. How much physical work have you performed?

sections.content:
If you hold heavy boxes all day, you are totally exhausted in the evening. You worked hard, didn't you? Physics says: No! In physics, you only perform work if you move something with a force along a path. If nothing moves, physical work is equal to zero!

📖 The Smart Dictionary: The Formula
Work is measured in Joules (J), just like energy. The formula is:
W = F · s (Work = Force times Distance). Without a path (s = 0), there is no work!

🧱 The Wall Experiment

Attempt to push the box and then the wall. Observe when physical work is performed!

The box is waiting.

{{QUIZ_q1}}

sections.title: 2. Lifting Work: Up into the Heights!

quizzes.question: What happens to the object's energy when you perform lifting work on it?

sections.content:
When you lift your school bag from the floor onto the table, you perform lifting work. You need a force to overcome gravity and lift the bag up a certain distance. This gives the bag potential energy. So, work is the process in which energy is transferred!

🏗️ The Busy Crane

Click on "Lift" to perform lifting work. The steel beam gains potential energy as a result!

Beam is on the ground. W = 0 J.

{{QUIZ_q2}}

sections.title: 3. Frictional Work: Why we get warm

quizzes.question: Into what is the energy mostly transformed when frictional work is performed?

sections.content:
Ever slid down a rope and burned your hands? That's frictional work! When you pull an object over a rough floor, the surfaces rub against each other. The work you put in doesn't disappear but is converted into thermal energy.

🔥 The Friction Sled

Change the ground. See how much force (and thus work) is needed to pull the sled!

{{QUIZ_q3}}

sections.title: 4. The Golden Rule of Mechanics

quizzes.question: What is the Golden Rule of Mechanics?

answers.text: What is saved in force must be made up for in distance.
Whoever works a lot must eat a lot.

sections.content:
Imagine you have to load a heavy piano into a truck. Do you lift it directly up (a lot of force, short distance) or do you push it over a long ramp (little force, long distance)? Physics has a brilliant mnemonic for this: "What is saved in force must be made up for in distance." The work performed remains exactly the same in both cases!

📐 The Inclined Plane

Click on the buttons to bring the ball up. Compare force and distance!

Choose a path!

{{QUIZ_q4}}

sections.title: 5. Deformation and Acceleration Work

quizzes.question: You step on the gas pedal and your car gets faster. What work does the engine perform?

sections.content:
There are even more types of work! When you squeeze a rubber ball or stretch a bow, you change the shape – that is deformation work. When you pedal hard on your bike to get faster, that is acceleration work. In doing so, you increase the kinetic energy!

⚙️ The Strong Spring

farben.title: 🌈 The Secret of Colors 🎨
farben.subtitle: Why is the sky blue and a rose red? It all starts in the atoms and with tiny waves. Let's solve the mystery of colors together!

sections.title: 1. How Light is Born in the Atom

quizzes.question: What happens when an electron falls back to its cozy inner orbit?

sections.content:
Do you remember electrons? When you give energy to atoms (e.g., through heat or electricity), the electrons get very jittery. They make a quantum leap to a higher orbit. But they can't stay there!

📖 The Smart Word: Photons
When an electron falls back from its high orbit, it has to get rid of the energy. It spits out a tiny energy package: a photon. That is the light we see!

Electron falls back = light package (photon) is released!

{{QUIZ_farben_s1_q0}}

sections.title: 2. Wavelengths: The "Size" of Color

quizzes.question: Which light color has the shortest waves and thus the most energy?

sections.content:
Light moves in waves, just like water waves in the sea. The distance between two wave crests is the wavelength. And exactly this length determines which color we see!

sections.title: 3. The Prism: The Rainbow Trick

quizzes.question: Which color is hidden in white sunlight?

answers.text: All the colors of the rainbow!

sections.content:
White light (from the sun) is actually a mixture of ALL colors! When white light flows through a glass triangle (prism), the colors are "refracted" to different degrees and sort themselves next to each other.

A prism separates white light into its colorful components.

optik1.subtitle: Why are there shadows? Why does the moon change its shape? Here you will learn all about the journey of light through space and time!

sections.title: 1. How Light Travels

quizzes.question: In what form does light normally travel?

sections.content:
Light is like a super-straight ruler. As long as nothing is in its way, it zooms straight through space. But if an opaque body (like you, a tree, or a stone) is in the way, the light can't pass. Behind it, an area without light is created: the shadow.

sections.title: 2. Umbra and Penumbra

quizzes.question: What is the penumbra?

answers.text: The area where light from only one of two lamps reaches.
The area where no light reaches at all.

sections.content:
What happens when we use two lamps? Each lamp casts its own shadow. Where both shadows overlap, it is pitch dark – that is the umbra. In the gray areas next to it, a little light from one of the two lamps still arrives – that is the penumbra.

sections.title: 3. Shadows in Space: Eclipses

quizzes.question: What happens during a solar eclipse?

answers.text: The Earth casts its shadow on the sun.
The moon casts its shadow on the Earth.

sections.content:
Planets and moons also cast giant shadows. During a solar eclipse, the moon moves in front of the sun and casts its umbra on the Earth. During a lunar eclipse, the moon moves through the shadow of the Earth.

sections.title: 4. Reflection: The Echo of Light

quizzes.question: What is the law at the mirror?

answers.text: Angle of incidence = Angle of reflection.

sections.content:
When light hits a smooth surface (mirror), it bounces off. The following applies: The angle at which the light arrives (angle of incidence) is exactly the same as the angle at which it jumps away (angle of reflection). On rough walls, the light is scattered – that's why a wall doesn't reflect.

sections.title: 5. Diffraction: When Light Becomes a Wave

quizzes.question: What happens at a very narrow slit?

answers.text: The light spreads out in a circular pattern behind it (diffraction).

sections.content:
At very narrow edges, light shows its wave nature. Christiaan Huygens discovered: Every point of a wave can emit new spherical waves. The light "bends" a bit around obstacles (diffraction).

astronomie.title: 🌌 The astrophysics adventure 🚀
astronomie.subtitle: Hello space explorers! Buckle up. We leave Earth and travel to black holes, exploding stars and the boundaries of space and time!

sections.title: 1. Cosmic dimensions: How small are we really?

quizzes.question: What unit of measurement do astronomers often use for distances in our solar system?

sections.content:
On Earth, a mountain seems huge to us. But in space, the Earth is just a tiny speck of dust. When we look into space, we have to get used to completely new dimensions. Jupiter is so big that Earth would fit over 1,300 times. And our sun? A gigantic fireball!

📖The clever space dictionary:
Because kilometers in space are far too small numbers, astronomers measure inAstronomical units (AU). 1 AU is the distance from the Earth to the Sun (about 150 million kilometers).

sections.title: 2. The speed of light: The absolute speed limit

quizzes.question: What exactly is a "light year"?

answers.text: The time it takes to fly to the sun.
The distance that light travels in a year.

sections.content:
Nothing in the universe is faster than light. It's racing at incredible speeds300,000 kilometers per secondthrough space! When you turn on a flashlight, the light is on the wall almost immediately. But space is so huge that even the extremely fast light takes time.

📖The light year:
A light year isnotime, but oneRoute! It is the distance that light travels in a whole year (almost 9.5 trillion kilometers).

sections.title: 3. Gravity: When mass bends space

quizzes.question: Why is a black hole called "black"?

answers.text: Because its gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.
Because it is made of dark charcoal.

sections.content:
Why don't we fall off the earth? Because of gravity (gravity)! Albert Einstein discovered that every heavy body (like a kind of bowling ball on a trampoline) bends the space around it. The heavier something is, the stronger it attracts other things.

📖The Black Hole:
When a giant star dies, it can collapse. It becomes infinitely small but retains its enormous mass. Gravity becomes so extreme there that not even light can escape - a black hole is born!

sections.title: 4. Escape Velocity: Off to Space!

quizzes.question: What does a rocket have to achieve in order to leave Earth permanently?

sections.content:
Gravity holds us down. If a rocket wants to fly into space, it has to be incredibly fast in order to escape the Earth's gravitational pull. This speed is calledescape velocity. For Earth it is approx.11.2 kilometers per second(around 40,000 km/h!).

📖The rocket equation:
To go that fast you need a lot of fuel. But fuel is heavy! The more fuel you pack, the heavier the rocket becomes and the more thrust you need. A nasty cycle!

quizzes.question: What happens during a supernova?

answers.text: A huge star explodes at the end of its life.

sections.content:
Stars don't live forever. Inside they burn hydrogen to helium (nuclear fusion). This makes them glow. But at some point you run out of fuel! With very massive stars, gravity suddenly wins: the star collapses and hits its own core. The result? The most powerful explosion in the universe:A supernova!

force_and_motion.title: 🚀 The Force Adventure ⚡
force_and_motion.subtitle: Hello Physics Astronaut! Buckle up, we're exploring the invisible forces that move our world!

sections.title: 1. Inertia: The Inner Slacker of Things!

quizzes.question: Why does a soccer ball on the grass stop eventually, but an asteroid in space keeps flying forever?

answers.text: On the grass, a force (friction) slows it down. In space, there's nothing to slow it down.
Because the ball on Earth eventually runs out of breath and gets tired.

sections.content:
Have you ever wondered why you fly forward in a car when it brakes hard? That's called inertia. Things are pretty lazy! A ball sitting still on the ground wants to stay there forever. A ball flying through space wants to fly forever. It only changes its mind if a force (like a kick or a wall) forces it to!

📖 The clever dictionary: Sir Isaac Newton
The clever researcher Isaac Newton was the first to write this down correctly. His 1st Law states: "An object remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by a force."

⚽ The lazy soccer ball

Give the ball a nudge in space (no air, no ground). It won't stop flying!

{{QUIZ_q1}}

sections.title: 2. Friction: The Invisible Brake

quizzes.question: Why do you slide much better with socks on tiles than on a thick wool carpet?

answers.text: Because the carpet creates much more friction, which slows you down.
Because tiles are colder and cold creates a slippery force.

sections.content:
But why do things on Earth always stop then? Because of friction! When two surfaces rub against each other, their tiny, microscopic unevenness hook into each other. This slows down the movement and even generates heat (try rubbing your hands together quickly!).

📖 The clever dictionary: Lubricants
When we want things to slide better, we use lubricants like oil or water. They fill the tiny gaps so the surfaces slide past each other almost as if on roller skates!

🧊 The slide race: Ice vs. Carpet

Push both blocks with exactly the same force!

sections.title: 3. Gravity: The Invisible Leash

quizzes.question: What would happen if you dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon (where there is no air) at the same time?

answers.text: Both fall at exactly the same speed to the ground.
The hammer falls much faster because it is heavier.

sections.content:
Every thing in the world attracts other things. The heavier something is, the stronger it pulls! You attract your computer, but you're too light for it to be noticed. But the Earth is GIGANTICALLY heavy. It pulls you, me, houses, and apples towards it with full force. We call this attractive force gravity.

📖 Mass vs. Weight
Your mass (how many particles you are made of) is the same everywhere. But your weight changes! On the Moon, gravity is weaker. There you suddenly weigh 6 times less and could make huge jumps, even though you are still made of the same number of particles!

🍎 The parachute experiment

Gravity pulls everything down at the same speed! Only air resistance slows down light, flat things like feathers. Let's turn off the air (vacuum)!

{{QUIZ_q3}}

sections.title: 4. Action and Reaction: Recoil

quizzes.question: You blow up a balloon and let it go without tying it. What happens?

answers.text: It falls immediately like a stone to the ground.
The air shoots out the back (action) and the balloon flies wildly forward as a reaction.

sections.content:
Nature is very fair! When you exert a force on something, that something pushes back on you with the exactly same force. If you push off a wall on roller skates (action), the wall pushes you back and you roll backwards (reaction).

📖 Rockets in Space
How can a rocket fly in empty space if it can't "push off" anywhere? It pushes off its own fuel! The rocket throws extremely fast, hot gases out the back (action). This pushes the rocket forward as a reaction!

🚀 Rocket Launch

{{QUIZ_q4}}

sections.title: 6. Newton's 2nd Law: F = m · a

quizzes.question: What happens if you exert the same force on a MUCH heavier object?

sections.content:
Newton found another important law. It explains how force, mass, and acceleration are related: Force = mass times acceleration (F = m · a). This means: If you want to accelerate something very heavy (lots of mass) quickly, you need a huge force!

📖 The clever dictionary: Acceleration
Acceleration (a) doesn't just mean getting faster. Braking or cornering is also an acceleration because the speed or direction changes. For every change, you need a force (F)!

🏎️ The Acceleration Race

Choose a vehicle and step on the gas (same force)! Who picks up speed faster?

Choose a starter!

{{QUIZ_q_newton2}}

sections.title: 7. Types of Friction: Static, Sliding, Rolling

quizzes.question: Which friction is usually the smallest (easiest to overcome)?

sections.content:
Friction is not all the same. There are three stages:

  1. Static friction: The hardest moment. You push against a cabinet, but it doesn't move yet. The particles "hook" together firmly.
  2. Sliding friction: Once the cabinet starts sliding, it gets a bit easier.
  3. Rolling friction: The pro trick! If you put rollers under the cabinet, the friction becomes tiny.

📦 Cabinet Transport

Try to move the heavy cabinet. Which method is best?

{{QUIZ_q_friction_types}}

sections.title: 5. The Lever: Strong as a Bear

quizzes.question: What do you have to do if you want to lift a very heavy stone with a crowbar?

answers.text: Grip the bar very far back so that my lever arm is nice and long.
Grip the bar very close to the stone.

sections.content:
Sometimes our own muscle power is simply not enough to move something heavy. A trick helps us: The lever! A lever is basically just a bar and a fulcrum. If you make the side of the bar where you push very long, you can suddenly lift things that are much heavier than yourself!

📖 The golden law of the lever
"Force times effort arm equals load times load arm". That sounds complicated, but it just means: If your arm of the seesaw is twice as long, you only need half the force to push!

linsen_spiegel.title: 🌈 The Optics Adventure 🔦
linsen_spiegel.subtitle: Welcome, young researchers! Buckle up, we're traveling on a beam of light through the exciting world of optics!

sections.title: 1. Reflection: Ping-Pong with Light

quizzes.question: What do you call the invisible auxiliary line that stands perpendicular to the surface when reflecting?

sections.content:
Light particles often behave like perfect little bouncy balls. If you throw a bouncy ball diagonally against a smooth wall, it bounces back in the other direction at exactly the same angle. Light does exactly the same at a smooth mirror! In physics, this bouncing back is called reflection.

📖 The Smart Dictionary: The Law of Reflection
To measure how diagonally the light hits the mirror, physicists draw an invisible auxiliary line exactly perpendicular (at a 90-degree angle) to the mirror. This line is called the normal.
The angle between the incoming light ray and the normal is called the angle of incidence. The law of nature is super simple: Angle of incidence = Angle of reflection!

🎮 The Laser Mirror

Move the slider to aim the laser flatter or steeper at the mirror:

{{QUIZ_q1}}

sections.title: 2. Refraction: The Bend in Optics

quizzes.question: Why does the light ray bend when it hits the water at an angle?

answers.text: Because water is optically denser and slows down the light.
Because the water is wet and washes the light away.

sections.content:
Light is incredibly fast in empty space. But when it travels through materials like water or thick glass panes, it has to work harder and is slowed down slightly. When a light ray enters such a material at an angle, it suddenly changes its direction because of the slowing down. We call this refraction!

📖 The Smart Dictionary: Optical Density
Water and glass are harder to penetrate than air. They are said to have a higher optical density. Imagine you are running on asphalt and run diagonally into a pool full of modeling clay. The foot that steps into the clay first is immediately slowed down. The other foot still runs fast – as a result, you automatically pull a curve! This is exactly how the light bends towards the normal.

🧪 The Basin Lab

Select which material the laser beam should shine into:

Aktuell: Luft (Gleiche Dichte, Strahl geht einfach geradeaus)

{{QUIZ_q2}}

sections.title: 3. Total Internal Reflection: When Light is Trapped

quizzes.question: What happens to the light ray during total internal reflection?

answers.text: It is completely reflected back at the interface like in a mirror.

sections.content:
Imagine you are underwater and looking diagonally up at the surface. At a certain angle, something magical happens: the light can no longer leave the water! Instead, it is reflected back at the water surface like a perfect mirror. We call this total internal reflection.

📖 The Smart Dictionary: The Critical Angle
Total internal reflection only happens when light wants to go from an optically dense substance (like water or glass) into a thinner substance (like air) – and at a very flat angle. The angle at which this starts to happen is called the critical angle.

🔦 Das Licht im Glasstab

Move the laser. Beyond a certain angle, the light is no longer refracted, but totally reflected!

{{QUIZ_q_total}}

sections.title: 4. The Eye: Your Built-in Camera

quizzes.question: What does the lens of the eye do so that we see things nearby clearly?

answers.text: It becomes thicker and more curved.

sections.content:
Your eye works almost like a digital camera. In the front sits a lens that focuses the light and projects a sharp image onto the back wall of the eye (the retina). The crazy thing: on the retina everything is upside down! Your brain first has to flip the image back the right way.

📖 The Smart Dictionary: Accommodation
So that you can see both the cell phone right in front of your nose and the distant church tower clearly, your eye can change the shape of the lens. Muscles pull it flat (for the distance) or let it become thick (for the near). This trick is called accommodation.

👁️ Der Seh-Simulator

Your eye adapts: click on the objects to see how the lens changes shape!

Wähle eine Entfernung!

sections.title: 5. Lenses: Light Focusers and Diffusers

quizzes.question: Which lens do you use if you want to concentrate the light of the sun in one point like with a magnifying glass?

sections.content:
We humans use the trick of refraction by grinding glass into very specific, round shapes. We call these pieces of glass lenses. With them, we can build magnifying glasses, glasses, and cameras!

📖 Two Shapes, Two Tricks:
- Converging lens (convex lens): It is nice and thick and bulging in the middle. It catches light rays and directs them inwards until they all meet in a super hot point: the focal point (focus).
- Diverging lens (concave lens): It is thinner in the middle than at the edge. It pushes the rays outwards as if they were scattered.

💡 A great mnemonic: "Convex is like the back of a hex (bulging outwards), concave is like a deep sheep's grave (curved inwards like a cave)."

🔍 The Lens Swapper

Click to swap the lens:

Sammellinse (Konvex): Bündelt alle Strahlen im Brennpunkt!

{{QUIZ_q3}}

sections.title: 4. Diffraction: Light goes around the corner!

quizzes.question: When does the light diffract most strongly into new circular waves?

answers.text: When the gap is extremely narrow.
When the gap is open like a giant barn door.

sections.content:
We used to think that light rays always travel strictly in a straight line. But surprise: light actually behaves like a wave in the ocean! When this light wave hits an extremely tiny obstacle or a very narrow gap, it shows its magical nature.

📖 The Smart Dictionary: Diffraction (Huygens' Idea)
The scientist Christiaan Huygens discovered Huygens' principle. He said: Every tiny point of a light wave can create a completely new spherical wave! If a gap is extremely narrow, we force the light through it. Suddenly, the tiny gap acts like its own little lamp, and the light spreads out in a circle behind it. This is called diffraction.

🌊 The Slit Machine

Click on the box to make the gap progressively narrower:

Breiter Spalt: Das Licht geht fast nur als gerade Welle (Wellenfront) durch.

{{QUIZ_q4}}

sections.title: 5. Curved Mirrors: The Funhouse Cabinet

quizzes.question: Which outward-curved mirror often hangs at dangerous road intersections because you can see a very wide field with it?

sections.content:
Thick glass lenses are often quite heavy! That's why we sometimes just use curved metal mirrors. They behave surprisingly similar to our lenses.

📖 The Mirror-Lens Twin:
- Concave mirror: Light falls into the depression like into a soup spoon. It behaves like a converging lens! It focuses the light in front of it in a real focal point.
- Convex mirror: The light bounces off the round "belly" (like a Christmas tree ornament). It behaves like a diverging lens. The light fans out and creates a virtual focal point for our eye that seemingly lies behind the mirror!

🪞 The Mirror Cabinet

Click to turn the mirror:

Hohlspiegel (Konkav): Bündelt das Licht wie eine Sammellinse.

{{QUIZ_q5}}

sections.title: 6. The Microscope: Journey to the Smallest Animals

quizzes.question: How many lenses does a simple microscope need at least?

sections.content:
To enter the world of bacteria or cells, we put two lenses into a long tube, the body tube. The lower lens is very close to the specimen and is therefore called the objective. The upper lens is directly at the eye – that's the eyepiece.

📖 The Invisible Image:
The objective collects the light from the tiny sample and projects an inverted, magnified intermediate image floating freely in the middle of the tube. The eyepiece now acts like a strong magnifying glass that we point at this floating image. If the intermediate image is exactly at the violet focal point of the eyepiece, the image in the eye becomes razor-sharp!

👁️ View through the eyepiece

Unscharf!

💡 Fokus-Tipp: Passe erst Regler 1 an, bis das graue Zwischenbild gut im Tubus liegt. Schiebe dann Regler 2, bis der violette Fokuspunkt das Zwischenbild exakt berührt!
{{QUIZ_linsen_s6_q0}}

sections.title: 7. The Telescope: A Look at the Stars

quizzes.question: Which two parts does the famous Newton telescope (reflector) use to direct the light into our eye?

answers.text: A large primary mirror and a small secondary mirror.
A concave lens and a convex lens.

sections.content:
A telescope for astronomers doesn't have to magnify insanely much. It's much more important that it collects as much faint starlight as possible! For that, you need a telescope with a giant aperture.

📖 Why Mirrors Win Over Lenses:
The classic refracting telescope (we call it a refractor) uses glass lenses. But gigantic lenses weigh tons! The glass is flattened under its own weight and the image becomes distorted. In addition, thick lenses produce ugly chromatic aberrations (rainbow edges) at the edges.
That's why Isaac Newton built the first reflecting telescope (reflector). At the very back of the tube sits a huge, curved primary mirror made of metal. It focuses the light towards the front, where a small, slanted secondary mirror throws the light sideways into the eyepiece. Perfect for giant observatories!

🔭 The Observatory

sections.title: 1. SI Units: The Time Machine
sections.content:
In physics, we almost always calculate time in the base unit seconds (s). If you get a problem that mentions minutes or hours, you must convert them first!

💡 Conversion Tip:
1 minute = 60 seconds

sections.title: 2. Base Units: The Luggage Check (Mass)
sections.content:
Masses are most commonly given in kilograms (kg). Often, things are labeled in grams (g). To know how heavy everything is together, you must bring everything to the same unit!

💡 Conversion Tip:
1,000 grams (g) = 1 kilogram (kg)
Example: 500 g = 0.5 kg

🧳 Pack the Suitcase

sections.title: 3. Prefixes: The Laser Measuring Device
sections.content:
Kilo means thousand (1,000), milli means one thousandth (0.001). When you add lengths, they must have the same prefix, otherwise there will be chaos!

sections.title: 4. Formulas: The Speed Camera (v = s / t)
sections.content:
Now it's getting serious! The formula for speed is v = s / t (speed = distance / time). Sometimes you also have to rearrange the formula:
Calculate distance: s = v * t
Calculate time: t = s / v

sieinheiten.title: 📏 The Measurement and Math Adventure 📐
sieinheiten.subtitle: Hello, Number Juggler! Get ready, we are exploring the absolute world language of science: accurate measuring and calculating!

sections.title: 1. SI Units: The language everyone understands

quizzes.question: Why do scientists all over the world use SI units?

answers.text: So that everyone means exactly the same length, time or mass and there are no errors.

sections.content:
Imagine you are building a treehouse with a friend in America. You say: "We need a board that is 5 feet long." Your friend measures with his feet – but they are much smaller than yours! The board doesn't fit. To avoid exactly this chaos, scientists all over the world have agreed on a common system: The International System of Units (SI).

📖 The clever dictionary: Measuring means comparing!
When you measure, you always compare an object with a fixed standard. 1 meter is exactly the same length all over the world, whether in Germany, Japan, or on the moon!

📏 The Tape Measure Chaos

Measure the blue rectangle! Click the buttons to see how the tape measure changes.

sections.title: 2. The 7 Base Quantities: The Foundation of the World

quizzes.question: Which unit belongs to the base quantity "Mass"?

sections.content:
Everything you can measure in the universe can be put together from just 7 basic building blocks (base quantities). The most important three, which you need almost every day, are: Length (meter, m), Mass (kilogram, kg) and Time (seconds, s).

📖 The complete team of 7:
1. Length (meter) | 2. Mass (kilogram) | 3. Time (second)
4. Electric current (ampere) | 5. Temperature (kelvin)
6. Amount of substance (mole) | 7. Luminous intensity (candela)

⏱️ The Reaction Time Experiment

sections.title: 3. Prefixes: From Kilo to Milli

quizzes.question: How many grams are in a kilogram (kg)?

sections.content:
Sometimes meters or grams are simply impractical. An ant is tiny, the distance to America is huge! For this we have "prefixes". They are like magic multipliers: Kilo always means "1000 times as much" (1 kilometer = 1000 meters). Milli means "one thousandth" (very tiny).

📖 The most important prefixes:
- Milli (m) = 1 / 1,000 (millimeter = tiny)
- Centi (c) = 1 / 100 (centimeter = small)
- Kilo (k) = 1,000 (kilogram = a lot)
- Mega (M) = 1,000,000 (megabyte = huge!)

sections.title: 4. Formulas: The Secret Recipes of Physics

quizzes.question: What happens to your speed if you suddenly need MUCH MORE time for the same distance?

answers.text: The speed becomes smaller (I am slower).
The speed becomes larger (I am faster).

sections.content:
In physics, we don't write long novels, we use formulas! They are like a short recipe that shows how things are related. Let's take speed. It depends on how much distance you cover in a certain amount of time. The formula is: v = s / t (speed = distance divided by time).

📖 The Formula ABC:
Scientists are lazy when it comes to writing. They use letters:
- v stands for velocitas (Latin for speed)
- s stands for spatium (distance)
- t stands for tempus (time)

In a diagram, there are two axes (lines): the x-axis is usually at the bottom on the ground (horizontal), the y-axis stands like a tree trunk upwards (vertical). waermelehre.title: 🔥 The Heat Adventure 🌡️
waermelehre.subtitle: Hello Fire-Tamer! Get ready, we are exploring the hot (and cold) world of temperature!

sections.title: 1. What is Heat? The Great Shiver!

quizzes.question: What happens to the smallest particles of an object when it is strongly heated?

answers.text: They move much faster and wilder.
They get tired and stop moving.

sections.content:
Whether it's water, wood, or air – everything around us consists of tiny building blocks called particles. And these particles never sit still! They wiggle and shiver all the time. Heat is actually nothing more than movement! The hotter something is, the more wildly and quickly the particles race around. When it gets cold, they move very slowly.

📖 The Smart Dictionary: Absolute Zero
Is there a point where the particles completely freeze and don't move at all anymore? Yes! This is called "absolute zero". It lies at an icy -273.15 degrees Celsius. It doesn't get colder than that in the entire universe!

🔬 The Particle Microscope

Turn the temperature up and watch how the particles go crazy!

Temperature: 10°C (Cold)

{{QUIZ_q1}}

sections.title: 2. Heat Conduction: The Fast Spoon Rally

quizzes.question: Why do people often use wooden spoons instead of metal ones for cooking?

answers.text: Because wood conducts heat better into the soup.
Because wood is an insulator and the handle doesn't get hot, so you don't burn your fingers.

sections.content:
When you stir a hot cocoa, the spoon handle eventually gets warm. Why? The fast, hot particles in the cocoa nudge the particles at the bottom of the spoon. These nudge their neighbors, and so the "wiggle energy" travels up the spoon. This is called heat conduction.

📖 The Smart Dictionary: Conductors and Insulators
- Good heat conductors: Metals (like copper or iron) pass heat along lightning-fast. That's why cooking pots are made of metal!
- Poor heat conductors (insulators): Wood, plastic, or air hardly let heat through. That's why a winter jacket has many thick air cushions – so your body heat doesn't escape!

☕ The Hot Soup Experiment

We put a metal spoon and a wooden spoon into hot soup. Click on "Heat Up"!

The soup is still lukewarm.

{{QUIZ_q2}}

sections.title: 3. Thermal Radiation: Heat without Touch

quizzes.question: Why do houses in very hot southern countries often have white walls?

answers.text: Because white is easier to clean.
Because the white color deflects (reflects) the sun's thermal radiation.

sections.content:
Do you remember the vacuum in space (without air particles)? How then does the sun's heat reach us on Earth if there is nothing there to "conduct" the heat? The answer: thermal radiation (infrared light)! It travels like light lightning-fast through empty space and warms us up as soon as it hits our skin.

📖 Colors make the difference: Black vs. White
Dark things (like a black T-shirt) "swallow" thermal radiation (absorption) and quickly become extremely hot. Light things (like white snow) throw the rays back like a mirror (reflection) and stay cooler.

☀️ The Parking Lot Test

The sun is shining! Which car will get hot faster for getting in during summer?

Black: 20°C

White: 20°C

{{QUIZ_q3}}

sections.title: 4. Thermal Convection: Why Hot Air Can Fly

quizzes.question: Above a burning candle, you feel the heat much more strongly than next to it. Why?

answers.text: Because the heated air becomes lighter and rises upwards (thermal convection).

sections.content:
Warm particles move faster and need more space. Dadurch dehnt sich heiße Luft aus und wird "leichter" als die kalte Luft drumherum. What happens? The warm air rises upwards! This is called thermal convection. Cold air sinks downwards in return.

📖 The Hot Air Balloon Secret
A hot air balloon has no engine! The pilot only fires a huge gas burner. The air in the giant envelope becomes hot, expands, and pulls the basket into the sky as if by magic. If the air cools down, the balloon sinks again.

🎈 The Balloon Ride

Hold the button down (or click repeatedly) to fire the burner!

The balloon is on the ground.

sections.title: 5. States of Matter: Ice, Water, Steam!

quizzes.question: What is the process called when liquid water becomes invisible water vapor?

sections.content:
Heat can completely transform things! Almost every substance has three forms of appearance (states of matter): solid, liquid, and gaseous. This is again due to our particles! If they are very cold, they cuddle closely together and are rigid (ice). If it gets warmer, they loosen up and flow around (water). If it gets really hot, they fly wildly apart into the air (water vapor).

📖 The Magic Words of Physics:
- Solid to liquid = Melting (Snowman in the sun)
- Liquid to gaseous = Evaporating (Boiling pasta water)
- Gaseous to liquid = Condensing (Mirror fogs up during showering)

💧 The Water Machine

Change the temperature of water:

It is solid ice.

{{QUIZ_q5}}

sections.title: 6. Thermal Expansion: Everything spreads out!

quizzes.question: Why do concrete and steel bridges need to have small grooves (expansion joints)?

answers.text: So that rainwater can drain away better.
So that the bridge has room to expand in the hot summer without breaking.

sections.content:
Because particles wiggle faster when heated, they need more space to "dance". The result: objects expand when they get hot! This happens with solids, liquids, and gases. When it gets cold, they contract again.

📖 The Thermometer Secret
Old thermometers use exactly this trick. At the bottom is a red liquid (often alcohol). Wenn es draußen warm wird, dehnt sich die rote Flüssigkeit aus und steigt im dünnen Glasröhrchen nach oben. Wir lesen die Temperatur ab!

🌡️ The Thermometer Lab

Heat the thermometer with the slider and see what happens!

drehundstatik.title: 🎡 The Rotation and Balance Adventure ⚖️
drehundstatik.subtitle: Hello physics acrobat! Get ready, we're spinning around and finding our inner balance!

sections.title: 1. The Center of Gravity: The Golden Middle

quizzes.question: Why do tightrope walkers often balance with an extremely long and heavy pole?

answers.text: So they can hold onto birds in an emergency.
The pole shifts the center of gravity downwards and outwards, making them much more stable.

sections.content:
Why don't you just fall over when you're standing? Because your body is in balance! Every object (including you) has a magical point: the center of gravity. You can imagine that the entire force of gravity pulls exactly at this one point. As long as this point is exactly above your standing surface, you stand securely. If you lean too far forward... *Thump!*

📖 The crazy donut secret
The center of gravity doesn't always have to be inside the material of the object! Where is the center of gravity for a donut or a tire? Right, exactly in the middle – in the hole where there's nothing at all!

🎪 The Tightrope Walker Test

Move the artist's center of gravity! If you push it too far to the left or right (beyond the rope), he falls!

Perfectly balanced!

sections.title: 2. Torque: The Door Trick

quizzes.question: Why are wrenches often so long?

answers.text: So you don't have to stand so close to the dirty screw.
A long handle increases the distance to the pivot point, which increases the torque (you need less force).

sections.content:
To turn something (e.g., a screw or a door), you need not only force but also the correct distance from the pivot point (the hinge). Force × Distance = Torque! If you want to open a heavy door, you push at the very outside of the handle. Try opening it very close to the hinge – it's incredibly difficult!

📖 The clever dictionary: Archimedes
The wise Greek Archimedes knew this over 2000 years ago. He said: "Give me a fixed point (pivot), and I will move the world!" He meant: With an infinitely long lever/distance, you only need a tiny amount of force to turn everything!

🚪 The heavy castle gate

Where do you want to push to push open the door (top view)?

The gate is closed.

sections.title: 3. Types of Equilibrium: The Bowl and the Mountain

quizzes.question: A broom that you balance upright on your finger is in which type of equilibrium?

answers.text: Stable. It jumps back onto the finger by itself.
Unstable. One little wobble and it falls over!

sections.content:
Standing isn't always the same! There are three ways things can rest in equilibrium:

  • Stable: If you nudge it, it wobbles briefly but falls back into its secure position.
  • Unstable (Wobbly): A small nudge and it falls irrevocably.
  • Neutral (Indifferent): If you nudge it, it simply stays at the new position (like a ball on flat ground).

sections.title: 4. Centrifugal Force: The Chain Carousel

quizzes.question: What happens to the centrifugal force when the carousel spins twice as fast?

answers.text: It becomes MUCH stronger! Whoever spins faster is pushed outward more strongly.
It becomes weaker because the wind from the movement pushes against it.

sections.content:
When you spin in a circle, you feel an invisible force pulling you outward. That's the centrifugal force! Actually, that's just our old friend inertia (from mechanics). Your body actually always wants to keep flying straight. But because the carousel forces you onto a circular path, it feels like you're being pushed outward!

📖 Driving through a curve in a car
If the car drives quickly into a sharp left turn, you are pushed to the right in your seat. Your body wants to keep going straight, but the car turns underneath you!

🎠 The Crazy Carousel

sections.title: 5. Angular Momentum: The Ice Skater Trick (Pirouette Effect)

quizzes.question: Why does a dancer spread her arms after a fast pirouette?

answers.text: To slow down the rotation by shifting mass outward.
To breathe in more air because she is dizzy.

sections.content:
Have you ever seen figure skaters on TV? When they spin on the ice and suddenly pull their arms close to their body, they spin lightning-fast like a tornado! This is called the pirouette effect (conservation of angular momentum). If you pull the mass inward, you automatically get faster. If you stretch your arms out again, you immediately slow down again!

⛸️ The Turbo Pirouette

Let the ice skater rotate and change the position of their arms!

The arms are stretched out. Rotation: Slow.

energie.title: ⚡ The Energy Adventure 🔋
energie.subtitle: Hello Energy Tamer! Get ready, we are exploring the invisible force that powers our universe!

sections.title: 1. What is Energy? The Invisible Engine!

quizzes.question: In which unit is energy measured?

sections.content:
Imagine you are lying lazily on the sofa. To get up and run into the room next door, you need something specific: Energy! Energy is the ability to move things, heat them up, or make them glow. You can't touch or weigh it, but you can see what it does. Without energy, absolutely nothing would happen in the entire universe – everything would stand still!

📖 The Smart Dictionary: Joule
Just as you measure distances in meters, you measure energy in Joule (J) (pronounced like "Jewel"). To lift an apple (approx. 100 grams) one meter high, you need about 1 Joule of energy!

🏋️ The Dumbbell Experiment (Potential and Kinetic Energy)

Lift the dumbbell to "store" energy in it (Potential Energy). Drop it to transform the energy into motion (Kinetic Energy)!

The dumbbell is on the ground. No energy stored.

sections.title: 2. The Great Magic Trick: Energy Transformation

quizzes.question: What does the Law of Conservation of Energy state?

answers.text: Energy cannot disappear, it only transforms into other forms.
You can create energy out of nothing if you try hard enough.

sections.content:
Now comes the most important thing you need to know about energy: Energy can never be created or destroyed! It only ever transforms from one form into another. This is called the Law of Conservation of Energy. When a light bulb glows, electrical energy is transformed into light energy (and heat). Nothing is lost!

📖 The Smart Dictionary: Forms of Energy
There are many "costumes" for energy:
- Kinetic Energy (A rolling car)
- Potential Energy (A stone on a mountain)
- Thermal Energy (A hot heater)
- Electrical Energy (Electricity in the socket)

⏱️ The Tireless Pendulum

Click on "Push". Observe how the pendulum has Potential Energy at the highest point, which transforms into Kinetic Energy as it falls!

sections.title: 3. Chemical Energy: The Power Snack

quizzes.question: What form of energy is stored in an apple that you eat?

sections.content:
Where do YOU actually get your energy to run and play? From your food! In foods like apples, bread, or pasta, there is chemical energy. Your body works like a small engine: It burns this chemical energy and turns it into kinetic energy and body heat. Chemical energy is also found in batteries or in the gasoline of cars!

📖 Calories = Energy!
On food packaging, you often see the word "Calories" (kcal). That is simply another unit for energy (1 kcal = approx. 4184 Joules). The more calories, the more energy is in the food!

🔋 The Hungry Flashlight

sections.title: 4. Where Does Our Electricity Come From? Renewable Energies

quizzes.question: Why are wind power and solar energy called "renewable" energies?

answers.text: Because you can buy them new at the supermarket.
Because they are never used up and are infinitely available.

sections.content:
To power our TVs, cell phones, and lamps, we need an enormous amount of electrical energy. In the past, coal or oil were burned for this (fossil fuels). The problem: This creates bad air (CO2) and eventually the coal runs out. Today we use more and more Renewable Energies! We use the power of wind, sun, and water. This energy never runs out and doesn't make a mess!

💨 The Wind Power Plant

sections.title: 5. The Electric Circuit: On the Electron Highway

quizzes.question: Why does a lamp not light up when the cable is cut?

answers.text: Because the circuit is interrupted and the electrons can no longer flow.
Because the electrical energy in the cable evaporates.

sections.content:
For electrical energy to work, it needs a closed path – the electric circuit. Electricity consists of tiny particles (electrons) that zip through copper cables. But watch out: They only flow if the circuit is completely closed, like a race track! If the cable is broken or a switch is open, all electrons stop immediately and the device turns off.

💡 The Light Switch

People used to think that electricity and magnets had nothing to do with each other. But in 1820, Hans Christian Ørsted noticed that a compass needle deflects when held next to a wire carrying an electric current.

elektrizitaet.title: ⚡ Das Strom-Abenteuer ⚡
elektrizitaet.subtitle:
Hallo! Schön, dass du da bist. Hier lernst du Schritt für Schritt, wie Elektrizität funktioniert.
        Lies dir die Erklärungen gut durch, schau dir die Bilder an, mache die kleinen Übungen und teste dein Wissen in den Quizzes.
        Für jede richtige Aktion sammelst du Punkte! Viel Spaß!

sections.title: 1. Die unsichtbaren Teilchen (Ladungen)

quizzes.question: Ein Elektron (-) und ein Proton (+) treffen sich:
1. Welche Teilchen sind negativ geladen und können sich leicht bewegen?

sections.content:
Alles um uns herum besteht aus winzigen Bausteinen, den Atomen. In diesen Atomen leben noch kleinere Teilchen, die eine elektrische Ladung haben. Stell sie dir wie kleine, geladene Bälle vor.

Ein Atom: Der schwere, positive Kern in der Mitte und die flinken, negativen Elektronen außen herum.

  • 🔴 Protonen: Diese sind positiv (+) geladen. Sie sind schwer, sitzen fest im Atomkern und bewegen sich fast nie.
  • 🔵 Elektronen: Diese sind negativ (-) geladen. Sie sind winzig klein und absolute Wirbelwinde. Sie flitzen auf Bahnen um den Kern herum!

Die allerwichtigste Regel der Elektrizität lautet:
Gleiches mag sich nicht (stößt sich ab). Aber Gegensätze ziehen sich an!

Die Grundregel: Gleiche Ladungen wollen weg voneinander, ungleiche wollen zueinander.

__PH0__ __PH1__

sections.title: 2. Was ist Strom eigentlich?

quizzes.question: Ein Stück Gummi (z.B. ein Radiergummi):
1. Warum ist das Kabel von deinem Handy-Ladegerät außen aus Plastik?

answers.text: Weil Plastik ein Isolator ist. Es verhindert, dass wir einen Stromschlag bekommen.
Weil es schöner aussieht und sich besser anfühlt.

sections.content:
Stell dir einen Fluss vor, in dem Wasser fließt. Elektrischer Strom ist genau das Gleiche – nur dass kein Wasser fließt, sondern Milliarden von kleinen, negativen Elektronen (-).

Strom ist also einfach nur: Bewegte Elektronen, die alle in die gleiche Richtung durch ein Kabel flitzen.

Wie Wasser im Rohr: Viele kleine Elektronen fließen gemeinsam durch das Kabel.

Damit sie fließen können, brauchen sie einen Weg (ein Kabel). Aber Achtung, nicht jedes Material lässt Elektronen durch!

  • 🟢 Leiter: Das sind Materialien, in denen die Elektronen frei wie auf einer Rutschbahn gleiten können. (Beispiele: Kupfer, Eisen, Gold, Wasser).
  • 🔴 Isolatoren: Das sind "Elektronen-Gefängnisse". Sie halten die Elektronen fest, nichts kann fließen. (Beispiele: Plastik, Gummi, Holz, Glas).
__PH0__ __PH1__

sections.title: 3. Stromkreis & Widerstand

quizzes.question: Du baust einen Stromkreis, aber ein Kabel in der Mitte ist durchgeschnitten (die Drahtenden berühren sich nicht). Was passiert?
1. Was passiert, wenn Strom durch einen Draht mit sehr hohem Widerstand fließt?

answers.text: Der Draht bremst die Elektronen und wird dabei warm.

sections.content:
Damit eine Lampe leuchten kann, müssen die Elektronen im Kreis fließen können. Sie starten bei der Batterie, fließen durch die Lampe und müssen wieder zurück zur Batterie kommen. Das nennt man einen geschlossenen Stromkreis.

Ein geschlossener Stromkreis: Der Strom kann im Kreis fließen.

Die Strom-Bremse (Widerstand): Auch in einem super Leiter (wie Kupfer) fließen die Elektronen nicht völlig frei. Das Material bremst sie etwas ab. Ein dünnes Kabel bremst stärker als ein dickes Kabel. Wenn sich die Elektronen durch ein dünnes Kabel quetschen müssen, reiben sie aneinander und das Kabel wird heiß. Genau so funktioniert ein Toaster!

__PH0__ __PH1__

sections.title: 4. Die Batterie: Die Strom-Pumpe

quizzes.question: Wie heißt der Teil in der Batterie, der den direkten Weg für die Elektronen versperrt?
1. Wo starten die Elektronen ihre Reise durch den Stromkreis?

answers.text: Am Minuspol (Anode), weil es dort zu viele Elektronen gibt.

sections.content:
Elektronen sind ein bisschen faul. Sie fließen nicht einfach von selbst los. Sie brauchen einen "Schubs". Diesen Schubs nennt man elektrische Spannung. Eine Batterie ist wie eine Pumpe, die diesen Schubs erzeugt.

Das Innere einer Batterie: Die Chemie sorgt für den Ladungsunterschied.

  • 🔴 Die Anode (Minuspol): Hier entstehen durch Chemie ganz viele freie Elektronen. Hier ist es also extrem voll!
  • 🟢 Die Kathode (Pluspol): Hier herrscht Elektronen-Mangel. Die Elektronen wollen unbedingt hier rüber.
  • 🔵 Der Elektrolyt: Das ist eine dicke Paste in der Mitte. Er ist wie eine Mauer! Die Elektronen können nicht einfach direkt im Inneren rüberfliegen. Sie müssen den langen Umweg außen durch das Kabel (und durch unsere Lampe) nehmen!
__PH0__ __PH1__

sections.title: 5. Der Kondensator: Der Energie-Speicher

quizzes.question: 1. Was ist das Besondere an einem Kondensator im Vergleich zu einer Batterie?

answers.text: Er liefert über viele Stunden gleichmäßig Strom.
Er kann Energie sehr schnell auf einmal abgeben (z.B. für einen Blitz).

sections.content:
Ein Kondensator speichert Energie, aber anders als eine Batterie. Er funktioniert eher wie ein gespannter Bogen oder ein Staudamm.

Er besteht aus zwei Metallplatten, die sich nicht berühren. Dazwischen ist ein Isolator (z.B. Luft). Wenn wir Strom hineinpumpen, sammeln sich die Elektronen auf der einen Platte an. Sie wollen zur anderen, positiven Platte rüber, aber der Isolator versperrt den Weg! Die Spannung steigt an.

Ein geladener Kondensator: Die Ladungen stehen sich gegenüber, getrennt vom Isolator.

Die Energie ist jetzt gespeichert. Der Clou: Wenn man den Kondensator z.B. an eine Blitzlicht-Lampe anschließt, kann er die gesamte gespeicherte Energie blitzschnell auf einen Schlag abgeben!

__PH0__

sections.title: 6. Das Ohmsche Gesetz: U, I und R

quizzes.question: Was passiert mit der Stromstärke (I), wenn du die Spannung (U) erhöhst, aber der Widerstand gleich bleibt?

answers.text: Die Stromstärke wird größer (mehr Elektronen fließen).

sections.content:
Wie hängen Spannung, Stromstärke und Widerstand zusammen? Der Physiker Georg Simon Ohm hat die Antwort gefunden! Er entdeckte das Ohmsche Gesetz. Es ist wie eine Dreier-Beziehung:

  • Spannung (U) in Volt: Der Druck, der die Elektronen schiebt.
  • Stromstärke (I) in Ampere: Wie viele Elektronen pro Sekunde durchfließen.
  • Widerstand (R) in Ohm: Wie stark der Draht die Elektronen ausbremst.

Die Formel lautet: U = R · I (Spannung = Widerstand mal Stromstärke). Das bedeutet: Mehr Druck (U) macht mehr Strom (I)! Ein hoher Widerstand (R) macht weniger Strom (I).

⚡ Der Ohm-Rechner

Verändere Spannung und Widerstand. Beobachte, wie hell die Lampe leuchtet!

Spannung (U): 6V
Widerstand (R): 50 Ω

dgb5.title: 💻 Digital Basics 🖥️
dgb5.subtitle: Welcome to the digital world! Here you will learn everything you need to know about computers, the internet, and staying safe online.

sections.title: 1. Hardware & Software

quizzes.question: What is considered hardware?

sections.content:
Computers consist of Hardware (things you can touch) and Software (programs and apps).

{{QUIZ_dgb_s1_q1}}
